title: Isis and Osiris (Moralia V, Loeb Classical Library 306), section 33
venue: Harvard University Press / Loeb Classical Library (scan on Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What do the earliest attestations of the words chemeia / chymeia say (e.g. Zosimus, Suda, Plutarch's Isis and Osiris use of Chemia for Egypt)?
quote: they call by the same name as the black portion of the eye, “Chemia,” and compare it to a heart
summary: Plutarch (c. AD 100) reports that the Egyptians call their land, which has very black soil, Chemia (Greek text read: Χημίαν καλοῦσι), likened to the black of the eye and to a heart. Earliest opened attestation of Egypt = Chemia; it concerns the country name, not the art of alchemy.
limits: Says nothing about metals or transmutation; does not by itself show the later word chemeia derives from this name. Loeb translation from 1936; OCR text of the scan.

title: The Origins of Alchemy in Graeco-Roman Egypt (philology of Chemeia, black-soil section)
venue: Frederick Muller, London (scan on Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
quote: Philologically then there is not much to be said for the interpretation of Chemeia as the Black or Egyptian Art.
summary: Lindsay sets out the kmt 'black land' derivation (Coptic Kime/Khime, Plutarch's Chemia) and judges it philologically weak, while allowing that practitioners may have felt an echo between Khime and Chymia. He treats the geographical black-land reading of Plutarch as likelier than 'Black Art'.
limits: Author is a literary historian and novelist rather than a trained philologist; 1970 and pre-dates later scholarship. Also discusses and rejects as 'highly farfetched' a derivation from the Egyptian kmj.f (Book of Wisdom).

title: The Origins of Alchemy in Graeco-Roman Egypt (chyma, 'to pour', section on the name alchemy)
venue: Frederick Muller, London (scan on Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
quote: this fact gives it a great claim to underlie the name of Alchemy.
summary: Argues chymia/chymeia comes from Greek cheein 'pour' and chyma 'ingot, bar' (attested 3rd-century BC Oropos inscription, 2nd-century Delos), so the name arises from metallurgy. Notes that the earlier form of the word cannot be proved because no early texts exist.
limits: Secondary, 1970; the inscriptional evidence is reported, not examined here. Not a consensus statement; Lindsay himself says there is no proof which form was earlier.

title: Alchemy (word-origin and Diocletian sections) in Pseudoscience: A Critical Encyclopedia
venue: Greenwood Press / ABC-CLIO (scan on Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
quote: The word alchemy has its roots in the Greek chemeia, itself a derivation of the word for smelting metals.
summary: A sceptical reference work gives the Greek-metallurgical derivation of chemeia and the Arabic al-kimiya step as the standard account, and cites Newman & Principe 1998 for further reading. Does not mention the Egyptian black-land theory in the passage read.
limits: Brief encyclopedia entry for a general audience; no argument or primary evidence. The Newman and Principe article was cited but not opened.

title: χυμεία (Wiktionary, Ancient Greek etymology)
ask_addressed: What do the earliest attestations of the words chemeia / chymeia say (e.g. Zosimus, Suda, Plutarch's Isis and Osiris use of Chemia for Egypt)?
quote: it was named from its supposed inventor
summary: Gives the ancient tradition (Zosimos) that the art was named from an inventor Chymes, but says it is 'more probably' formed from χύμα (ingot, fluid) plus the suffix -εία. A dictionary shows the working lexicographic view, not original research.
limits: User-edited wiki; read as raw wikitext, so the quote is the plain-text part of the sentence. Cites no source in the part read.

title: Etymology of chemistry
ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
quote: this theory may be an example of folk etymology
summary: Reports the Egyptian (Budge: Coptic kēme, Demotic kmỉ, kmt) and Greek (khuma/khéō) derivations, attributes the folk-etymology warning to Friedrich Mahn via the OED, and notes Arabic al-kīmiyāʾ. Names no winner.
limits: Wikipedia is tertiary and user-edited; used as a finding aid, not as authority. Several claims tagged citation needed; Mahn and Budge are second-hand through this page.

title: Zosimos of Panopolis (Syncellus quotation on 'chema')
ask_addressed: What do the earliest attestations of the words chemeia / chymeia say (e.g. Zosimus, Suda, Plutarch's Isis and Osiris use of Chemia for Egypt)?
quote: for they called this book chema and hence the science of chemistry takes its name
summary: Quotes a passage preserved in Syncellus (Chronography) in which Zosimos ties the first tradition of the arts to a book called chema, from which chemistry takes its name. This is the ancient folk etymology and is independent of the kmt theory.
limits: Wikipedia is tertiary and user-edited; used as a finding aid, not as authority. The Greek was not opened; the passage is via a 1818 translation and Wikipedia's rendering.

title: Alchemy (etymology section, Diels 1914)
ask_addressed: What is the evidence and scholarly status of the claim that the word 'chemistry'/'alchemy' derives from Kemet/Khem/'black land' (Egyptian kmt)? What are the competing etymologies (Greek chyma/cheo, Arabic kimiya, others) and who argues which? State clearly which is most widely accepted and why.
quote: Hermann Diels argued in 1914 that it rather derived from χύμα
summary: Reports Hermann Diels's (Antike Technik, 1914) Greek derivation from chyma (cast metal), the main alternative to the Egyptian reading, and that others trace the word to Egyptian kēme 'black earth'.
limits: Wikipedia is tertiary and user-edited; used as a finding aid, not as authority. Diels was not opened; the citation is via Wikipedia.
